survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This factsheet reports descriptive PISA 2022 results for Sweden using the OECD PISA 2022 Database tables (e.g., I.B1.5.4–I.B1.5.6 for trends and I.B1.2.1–I.B1.2.3 for mean performance). The note does not describe the application of student/sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures, and it does not present any student-level model estimation. PISA results are produced under a complex sampling design with uncertainty intervals (95% confidence intervals) and technical standards; analysts using the underlying microdata should apply the official PISA sampling weights and replicate weights provided in the database to obtain correct standard errors. Because this document is a reporting factsheet rather than an analysis paper, the specific weight variable names and replicate method are not stated here.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This document is a descriptive results factsheet that reports PISA performance levels, mean scores, and trend comparisons using OECD database tables rather than fitting an analysis model on student microdata in the text provided. Plausible values are therefore not handled explicitly in this factsheet because the reported outcomes are already scaled/aggregated by the OECD PISA scaling process. Missing-data handling is also not described because the factsheet does not report any original estimation procedure or imputation strategy; it relies on the OECD PISA database products that already incorporate the assessment’s standard processing.

It also states that all data met PISA quality standards for Sweden, implying no exclusion due to failing sampling standards; however, the note does not detail additional analytic filtering beyond the standard PISA participation and completion requirements.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD PISA 2022 Sweden factsheet summarizes how 15-year-old students in Sweden performed in mathematics, reading, and science, and how results changed over time (notably between 2018 and 2022, and across 2012–2022). It reports mean performance trends, proficiency-level distributions (e.g., shares at Level 2 and Level 5/6), and gaps by socio-economic status, gender, and immigrant background, alongside contextual indicators such as belonging, safety, parental involvement, and COVID-related learning disruptions. For Sweden, 73% of students reached at least Level 2 in mathematics (OECD average: 69%) and 10% were top performers (Level 5 or 6), with similar reporting for reading and science (76% at Level 2+ in both reading and science; 10% top performers in each). The note also highlights widening gaps in mathematics and science between 2018 and 2022 for the top and bottom deciles of performance, and it reports that socio-economic status explains 15% of variation in mathematics performance in Sweden. The document is descriptive and does not provide an ML modeling pipeline, so no predictive metrics or causal claims are made; uncertainty is communicated via 95% confidence intervals and PISA technical standards.
